info.title: Test Helper API
info.description: Helper endpoints for end-to-end and load test automation: shared test-data lists, regional names, locks, an email catcher and sender with attachment search, a webhook catcher, TOTP codes, QR codes, performance statistics and spoken utterances for voice interfaces. Every action answers GET; parameter names are case-insensitive; no authentication (except the SMS capture app's device key). An LLM-oriented guide is at {BASE_URL}/llms.txt. Import this document into Postman (Import > Link) to generate a collection. The same API in OpenAPI 3.0.3, for tools that do not read 3.2 yet: {BASE_URL}/openapi-3.0.json.

tags.name: lists
tags.description: Keyed test-data queues shared by every virtual user: push/pop/random records, bulk CSV/JSON import (atomic replace), run-scoped variables, atomic counters, and a cleanup register for records a test created.

tags.name: names
tags.description: Regional personas for test data: a female and a male name sharing a surname, with ASCII-folded forms. Repeatable with seed. 15 regions, in memory.

tags.name: mail
tags.description: Inbound mail catcher (any address at the mail domain, popped per address), outbound send through SES with generated, saved or received attachments, and an attachment store with text search inside PDF, Office and text files.

tags.name: sms
tags.description: Text messages: real texts caught by registered capture handsets (device-key protected), real sends to those handsets, and simulated texts to any other number.

tags.name: totp
tags.description: TOTP secret store and RFC 6238 code generation for MFA-protected test accounts.

tags.name: webhook
tags.description: Capture inbound webhooks from a system under test and read them back.

tags.name: lock
tags.description: Short-lived (60 s, no renew) mutual exclusion between concurrent test scripts that share one resource. Contention is 200 with locked:false.

tags.name: qr
tags.description: QR codes from text, as JSON (PNG as base64 and a data: URI), SVG, or a self-contained HTML page. Pure computation, no storage.

tags.name: perf
tags.description: Record performance data points from test scripts and read back exact counts, means and bounds, histogram percentiles (~2% relative accuracy), per-minute time series and pass/fail gates.

tags.name: voice
tags.description: Spoken utterances for testing voice interfaces: text with [tags] for emotion, pace and pauses becomes audio, stored by content so every request can be replayed byte for byte. Replay stored audio, pin it under a key, or keep a human recording beside it. Speech is Amazon Polly; each response says how faithfully each tag was rendered.

get.summary: Actions of lists
get.description: The service description and its action names.

get.summary: Append a record to a key's queue
get.description: Appends one record. Every query parameter other than `key` becomes a field of the record, stored as a string with its name exactly as sent (case kept). The fields `key`, `index` and `createdTime` are added to every record, so a parameter named `index` or `createdTime` is rejected (400). The key's queue is created on first use. Pushing onto a key filled by `lists/import` appends after the imported records.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: Every query parameter except key becomes a field of the record, with its value as a string (names keep the case you send). key, index and createdTime are reserved.

key.description: Caller-chosen namespace (a test run, team or data set). 1-128 characters: letters, digits and . _ - : @ + =, starting with a letter, digit or +. Case-sensitive.

email.description: Example record field. Any parameter except `key` is stored as a field.

get.summary: Take the next record (each record is handed out once)
get.description: Returns the record at the pop pointer and advances it in one atomic conditional write, so concurrent virtual users never receive the same record. When every record has been handed out the response is still HTTP 200, with `exhausted: true` and `record: null` - call `lists/reset` to start again. `remaining` is how many records are left after this one. For data that may be reused once every record has had its turn, use `lists/cyclepop`, which starts again at record 1 instead of running out.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Caller-chosen namespace (a test run, team or data set). 1-128 characters: letters, digits and . _ - : @ + =, starting with a letter, digit or +. Case-sensitive.

record.description: The record, or null when there is none.

get.summary: Take the next record, starting again at record 1 after the last (pop that never runs out)
get.description: Like `lists/pop`, but instead of running out it goes round again: after the last record it hands out record 1, then 2, and so on. One atomic write per call, so concurrent virtual users always get different records, and a record comes round again only after every other record has been handed out. It shares pop's pointer (`nextPop` in `lists/list`): `lists/reset` and `lists/import` start it at record 1 again, and after cyclepop has wrapped, a plain `pop` on the same key reports `exhausted` until a reset. `pass` counts the times round the list (1 on the first), `wrapped` is true on the first record of every pass after the first, and `remaining` is how many records are left in this pass. `exhausted` is true only when the key has no records at all (then `empty: true`, `record: null`, HTTP 200). Use it when a record may be reused but must not be in use by two scripts at once - keep the list larger than the number of scripts that can hold a record at the same time. Use `pop` when a record must never be used twice.

get.summary: Random uppercase alphanumeric codes (3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 characters)
get.description: Stateless; takes no parameters. Each call returns five independently generated random codes drawn uniformly from A-Z0-9. Pick the length that matches the uniqueness your test needs: `rand3` is human-memorable for tiny runs, `rand10` is effectively unique at any realistic test volume. Codes can be concatenated (rand4 + rand10). A `rand10` also makes a good per-run `key`.

get.summary: Save a run-scoped variable under a key
get.description: Creates or overwrites the variable `name` under `key`. `value` is required but may be empty. URL-encode it.

parameters.name: value

get.summary: Read a variable, optionally waiting for it to be set or to equal a value
get.description: Returns the variable's value (always a string). Without wait or equals, a variable that was never set is a 404. With wait and/or equals the answer is always 200: exists is false while the variable has never been set, and waitedMs says how long the request was held. With equals, matched says whether the value equals it (exact, case-sensitive). With wait=N the request is held up to N seconds and returns as soon as the value equals `equals`, or changes to something else (so a setup flag going from 0 to failed is reported at once); without equals, as soon as the variable exists. Reads are strongly consistent. Typical use - the test-cycle gate (llms.txt recipe 4.12): vars/get?key=<project>&name=setupReady&equals=1&wait=20, repeated until matched is true.

get.summary: Advance a counter atomically
get.description: Applies the increment with a single DynamoDB atomic ADD - no read first - so concurrent virtual users cannot lose each other's updates. Returns the value AFTER the change, which makes it usable as a sequence-number generator. One counter is one item, so it accepts roughly 1,000 increments per second; for unique values at load-test volume use `lists/codes`, which needs no coordination. A counter is created on first use.

parameters.description: Counter name within the key: 1-64 characters of letters, digits, '.', '_' or '-'. Defaults to `default`.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: Whole number to add; may be negative or zero. Default 1. Fractions are rejected.

get.summary: Read a counter without changing it
get.description: Returns the current value. A counter that has never been incremented reads as 0 with `exists: false` (not 404), so a script can read one before anything has written to it.

get.description: Call this from the create step of a test with whatever identifies the created record in the system under test. Entries are handed back by `lists/cleanup/pop` in the order they were saved. Duplicates are kept as separate entries: the same identifier created twice is two records to remove.

get.description: Returns ONE registered record at a time, oldest first, and stamps `removedTime` as it is handed over. The claim is a single conditional write, so two cleanup scripts running at once never receive the same record. Loop until `exhausted: true` (HTTP 200). Because the stamp happens on handover, a cleanup script that dies midway leaves those records marked removed - reconcile with `lists/cleanup/list` if that matters.

get.summary: Replace a key's records from an uploaded file (ref)
get.description: LOADING ALWAYS REPLACES: every record under the key is swapped for the file's records and the pop pointer rewound to 1, in one atomic metadata write, so readers see the old set or the new set, never a mix; a failed import changes nothing. The import runs in the background; the call waits up to `wait` seconds and answers 200 `state: done` with the result, 202 `queued`/`running` (poll `lists/import/status`), or 422 `failed`. Each record is returned by pop/random/list with its fields at the top level plus `key`, `index`, `createdTime` (a column or top-level property with one of those names is renamed `key_2` etc. and reported). CSV: the first row is the header; every value is text exactly as written (leading zeros kept); RFC 4180 quoting; comma/semicolon/tab/pipe auto-detected; UTF-8, Windows-1252 or UTF-16 detected; short rows padded (warning); rows with extra non-empty values skipped and reported by line; an unclosed quote fails the import. JSON: an array of objects, JSON Lines, an object wrapping one array ({"records": [...]}), or a single object (one record); JSON types kept; non-objects become {"value": ...}; integers beyond 2^53 kept exactly as strings. Limits: 4096 KB body, 50 MB via upload/url, 350 KB per record, 1,000,000 records. The file is kept 90 days for reload by ref. GET form: imports a file already uploaded with `lists/upload/url`, or reloads an earlier one.

get.summary: Actions of names
get.description: The service description and its action names.

get.summary: A female and a male persona for a region
get.description: Returns a female persona and a male persona (first, middle, last and composed full name) sharing one surname, drawn from curated in-memory lists for the chosen region. Every name field is also returned ASCII-folded under ascii, so a single call gives you both the true form and the folded one - useful for asserting that a system under test handles diacritics rather than silently mangling them; hasDiacritics says whether they differ. Poland's surnames inflect for women (Kowalski / Kowalska), flagged with genderedSurname. Japan and China write the family name first, flagged with familyNameFirst; a middle name is still returned for systems that demand one but is not part of the composed full name. Names only - no addresses, dates of birth or identifiers.

parameters.name: region
parameters.description: Region code, case-insensitive. One of AU NZ GB IE US CA DE FR ES IT NL PL IN CN JP, or ANY for no preference - see names/regions. Required unless notregion is supplied instead. An unknown code is a 404.

parameters.name: notregion
parameters.description: The inverse of region: choose a region at random from everywhere EXCEPT these. Comma-separated, so notregion=AU,NZ,GB excludes all three. Mutually exclusive with region. An unrecognised code is a 404 rather than a silent no-op. The response echoes excludedRegions and chosenFrom.

parameters.name: seed
parameters.description: Any string. The same seed always returns the same people - and with notregion or region=ANY the same region too, because the region is drawn from the seeded generator as well. Omit for a fresh random draw.

get.summary: List the available regions and their list sizes
get.description: Region codes with the number of female given, male given and family names held for each, plus the resulting combination count, whether the family name is written first, and whether surnames inflect by gender. List sizes vary by region because they are curated rather than padded. (Example shows the first two of 15.)

get.summary: Actions of mail
get.description: The service description and its action names.

get.summary: Take the next captured email for an address
get.description:
Returns the next unread message for `address` and advances the pointer. Any message sent to `<anything>@<mail domain>` is captured and queued per recipient address.

`attachments` is always a list of `{filename, ref, bytes}`; each `ref` is an opaque 10-character token into the temporary received-attachment store (7-day expiry) - use it with mail/attachments/get, mail/attachments/find, mail/attachments/save (to keep it) or mail/send (to forward it).

Nothing unread: 200 with `exhausted: true` and `body: null`. `pending: true` (also exhausted) means a message has been claimed by the receiver but is not written yet - call again, it has NOT been consumed.

`wait` holds the request open until a message arrives. With `wait`, `grace` defaults to 2: when nothing is unread, the most recently delivered message is offered again if it arrived within that many seconds, flagged `repeat: true`. This stops a message being missed in the gap between one polled request ending and the next starting. Do NOT use `wait` in a load test - each waiting call holds a concurrent Lambda execution for its whole duration.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Recipient address the mail was sent to (any local part at the mail domain). Case-insensitive.

parameters.name: wait
parameters.description: Seconds to hold the request open when the inbox is empty, returning the moment a message arrives. 0-20, default 0; larger values are clamped (API Gateway abandons a request at 29 s). Every response carries waitedMs.

parameters.name: grace
parameters.description: Seconds during which the most recently delivered message is re-offered (repeat:true) when nothing is unread. Default 2 when wait is used, 0 otherwise; max 60. Set grace=0 for strict one-message-per-call behaviour - a drain loop that pops until exhausted should do so.

get.summary: Rewind an address's pointer to its first message
get.description: Messages are kept; the next pop returns message 1 again. `reset: false` when the address has never received mail.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Recipient address the mail was sent to (any local part at the mail domain). Case-insensitive.

get.summary: Delete every captured email for an address
get.description: Deletes all messages and the pointer for `address`. `deleted` counts messages. Received attachments are not deleted here; they expire on their own after 7 days.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Recipient address the mail was sent to (any local part at the mail domain). Case-insensitive.

get.summary: Send an email (query-string form)
get.description:
Sends a real email through SES. Three forms:

* **GET** - everything in the query string, message in `body`.
* **POST, any non-JSON Content-Type** - the request body is the message.
* **POST, `Content-Type: application/json`** - structured: `{"body": "...", "attachments": [{"filename": "a.pdf", "key": "saved-key"}, {"ref": "rb0q4ipfcu"}]}` for several attachments (each item has exactly one of `key` or `ref`; `filename` optional). Cannot be combined with the attachment query parameters. A JSON-looking body sent WITHOUT the JSON content type goes out as literal text and the response carries `warning`.

Attachment caps: 28000 KB raw in total (SESv2 stops at 40 MB after base64). The recipient is the real limit: Outlook.com/iCloud 20 MB, Yahoo 25 MB, Microsoft 365 36 MB, Gmail 50 MB on the wire. Over 20 MB the response adds `deliverabilityWarning`, `messageMb` and `refusedBy`; it is still a 200 because SES accepted it - the refusal comes back later as a bounce. To test big attachments end to end, send to an address at the mail domain and pop it back.

`sentTime` (epoch seconds) is directly comparable with `receivedTime` from mail/pop. SES refusing the message is a 502.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Sender. Must be an address at the service's mail domain (or a subdomain of it) - the SES-verified identity. A display name is allowed: `Tester <test@example.com>`. Anything else is a 403.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Single recipient. Permitted: any address at the mail domain itself (so you can pop it straight back), or an address/domain on the deployment's allow-list (ALLOWED_TO / ALLOWED_DOMAINS; a `*.example.com` entry admits any subdomain but not example.com itself). Anything else is a 403 listing what is permitted.

parameters.name: subject
parameters.description: Subject line.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: Message text (plain). Required for GET.

parameters.name: attachmentkb
parameters.description: Attach a generated random-text file of exactly this many KB (1-6000). Mutually exclusive with key and ref.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Attach the SAVED attachment stored under this key (mail/attachments/save or upload/url). 404 if not found. Mutually exclusive with attachmentkb and ref.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: Attach a RECEIVED attachment straight from the temporary store (ref from mail/pop) - no need to save it first. 404 if expired. Mutually exclusive with attachmentkb and key.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Filename shown in the email ('.txt' appended if it has no extension). Defaults to the key, the received attachment's original filename, or a random name for generated text.

parameters.name: prepend64

get.summary: Search inside an attachment without downloading it
get.description:
Extracts text from the attachment and searches it, so a test can assert on document content without pulling the bytes into the harness. Handles PDF, docx/xlsx/pptx, and plain text / CSV / JSON / HTML; anything else falls back to printable-string extraction. Identify the file with `key` (saved) or `ref` (received).

PDF text is laid out as it appears on the page: one line per visual line, a tab between columns (label and value cells), a single space between words. Call `mail/attachments/text` to see exactly what is searched.

Exactly one search mode: literal (`text` / `text64`), regular expression (`regex` / `regex64`, Python syntax), or LoadRunner-style boundary capture (`left` + optional `right`, or `left64` / `right64`).

Whitespace is flexible by default: a space in `text`, `left` or `right` matches any run of spaces, tabs or line breaks, so `Invoice number INV-261002-1TFJP` matches across the column gap and `Total including GST` matches whether or not the label wraps. In boundary mode leading whitespace after `left` is skipped, captures are trimmed, and with no `right` the capture stops at the end of the cell (tab or line end). Empty captures are not counted (`emptyMatches`). `exact=true` restores character-for-character matching.

Password-protected PDFs: pass `password` (or `password64`). Either the user (open) or owner password works; PDFs with only an owner password (restrictions) open without one. RC4 40/128, AES-128 and AES-256 are supported. A missing or wrong password is 422 with `passwordRequired` or `passwordIncorrect`.

`in=metadata` searches the PDF document properties (Title, Author, Keywords and custom keys such as InvoiceNumber), one `Name<TAB>value` line each; `in=all` searches both. Every result has `page` (1-based; null for metadata or non-PDF files). Regex and boundary modes add `values`: the flat list of captures. A `count` of 0 adds `caseInsensitiveCount` and a `hint`. `document.characters` near zero means the document has no text layer (a scan, no OCR), not that the term is absent. Extraction (10 s) and matching (3 s) run under wall-clock guards and return 400 rather than a gateway timeout. Files over 20480 KB are refused (400).

get.description: The service description and its action names.

get.summary: Say text: text (with [tags]) to audio, stored by content
get.description:
Turns text into spoken audio, and stores it by content.

**Replay.** The whole request (words, tags, voice, engine, format, sample rate, pronunciations) is reduced to a canonical form and hashed; the hash is `ref` and the audio is stored under it. The same request returns the same audio byte for byte with `cached: true` and nothing is synthesised, so a failing test can be run again on exactly the stimulus it failed on, and a thousand virtual users saying the same words cost one synthesis. Generated audio is kept 30 days after its last use; `voice/save` keeps one for good.

**Tags.** Put ElevenLabs-style tags in square brackets where the delivery should change: `[anxious] I've been waiting. [pause] Is the doctor late?`. Emotions (`[anxious]`, `[angry]`, `[sad]`, `[relaxed]`, ...), pace (`[slowly]`, `[quickly]`), volume (`[softly]`, `[loudly]`, `[whispers]`), pauses (`[pause]`, `[long pause]`, `[pause 800ms]`) and sounds (`[sighs]`, `[laughs]`). A tag holds until the next tag of its kind; `[neutral]` clears them. Tags are never spoken. `voice/tags` lists them all.

**Honest rendering.** No AWS voice takes emotion as an instruction today. Each tag is rendered as well as the chosen engine can and reported in `tags[]`: `native`, `approximated` (a change of rate, pitch or volume), `inferred` (generative voices read emotion from the wording) or `none` (not audible; sounds such as `[sighs]`). With `strict=true` a request with any `none` tag is refused with 422 before anything is synthesised. `ssml` shows exactly what the engine was asked to say.

**The audio** comes back as base64 in `data`; `url=true` gives a presigned URL instead; `view=true` or `download=true` redirect to the audio, so the say URL itself works as an `<audio src>`; `play=true` returns a small page that plays it from script with no player on screen (and one Play button if the browser will not let a page make sound before a click). `format=wav&hz=16000` is the form microphones and speech-to-speech streams take; in `wav` and `pcm`, a pause at the very start or end is exact digital silence.

**POST** takes the same names as a JSON body, plus `segments` (each `{"text", "emotion"}` or `{"pause": ms}`, each starting from the utterance's own emotion) and `pronounce` (`{"word": "how to say it"}`). A form body (`curl -d 'text=...'`) is read as fields; any other body is taken as the text. A `text` that is a complete `<speak>` document is passed to the engine as written.

**Say it again.** `ref` (or the `key` of a saved utterance) in place of `text` says the stored script again with another `voice`, `engine`, `format` or `hz` - a new ref, the same words and direction.

New synthesis is capped per day on each deployment (429 with `budgetExhausted` when used up); stored audio is never affected.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: The words to say, with optional [tags]. Up to 3000 characters. Send text or text64.

parameters.name: text64
parameters.description: Base64 of the text (standard or URL-safe alphabet, padding optional). Use it when the text has + & % # or brackets your client will not encode.

parameters.name: emotion
parameters.description: One emotion word for the whole utterance: the same as that tag at the very start. voice/tags lists them.

parameters.name: voice
parameters.description: A voice name (voice/voices lists them), or random. Default: the deployment's voice (Olivia, Australian English). If that voice is not available on the engine asked for, the first voice by name in the same language is used.

parameters.name: language
parameters.description: A language code (en-GB) or a language on its own (en). Chooses the voice when voice is not given, and narrows voice=random.

parameters.name: engine
parameters.description: standard, neural (the default) or generative. Neural is stable and takes rate and volume; standard also takes pitch and a true whisper but sounds synthetic; generative sounds the most human, reads emotion from the wording and cannot be directed.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: mp3 (default), ogg, wav, pcm (raw 16-bit mono), mulaw or alaw.

parameters.name: hz
parameters.description: Sample rate. mp3/ogg: 8000, 16000, 22050 or 24000 (default 24000; 22050 for standard voices). wav/pcm: 8000 or 16000 (default 16000). mulaw/alaw: 8000.

parameters.name: seed
parameters.description: With voice=random: makes the choice of voice repeatable.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: true: refuse (422) if any tag would not be heard on this engine, instead of leaving it out.

parameters.description: true: return a presigned URL instead of base64 data.

parameters.description: true: answer with a redirect to the audio, played in the browser.

post.summary: Say text from a JSON body: segments, pronunciations, strict
post.description:
Turns text into spoken audio, and stores it by content.

**Replay.** The whole request (words, tags, voice, engine, format, sample rate, pronunciations) is reduced to a canonical form and hashed; the hash is `ref` and the audio is stored under it. The same request returns the same audio byte for byte with `cached: true` and nothing is synthesised, so a failing test can be run again on exactly the stimulus it failed on, and a thousand virtual users saying the same words cost one synthesis. Generated audio is kept 30 days after its last use; `voice/save` keeps one for good.

**Tags.** Put ElevenLabs-style tags in square brackets where the delivery should change: `[anxious] I've been waiting. [pause] Is the doctor late?`. Emotions (`[anxious]`, `[angry]`, `[sad]`, `[relaxed]`, ...), pace (`[slowly]`, `[quickly]`), volume (`[softly]`, `[loudly]`, `[whispers]`), pauses (`[pause]`, `[long pause]`, `[pause 800ms]`) and sounds (`[sighs]`, `[laughs]`). A tag holds until the next tag of its kind; `[neutral]` clears them. Tags are never spoken. `voice/tags` lists them all.

**Honest rendering.** No AWS voice takes emotion as an instruction today. Each tag is rendered as well as the chosen engine can and reported in `tags[]`: `native`, `approximated` (a change of rate, pitch or volume), `inferred` (generative voices read emotion from the wording) or `none` (not audible; sounds such as `[sighs]`). With `strict=true` a request with any `none` tag is refused with 422 before anything is synthesised. `ssml` shows exactly what the engine was asked to say.

**The audio** comes back as base64 in `data`; `url=true` gives a presigned URL instead; `view=true` or `download=true` redirect to the audio, so the say URL itself works as an `<audio src>`; `play=true` returns a small page that plays it from script with no player on screen (and one Play button if the browser will not let a page make sound before a click). `format=wav&hz=16000` is the form microphones and speech-to-speech streams take; in `wav` and `pcm`, a pause at the very start or end is exact digital silence.

**POST** takes the same names as a JSON body, plus `segments` (each `{"text", "emotion"}` or `{"pause": ms}`, each starting from the utterance's own emotion) and `pronounce` (`{"word": "how to say it"}`). A form body (`curl -d 'text=...'`) is read as fields; any other body is taken as the text. A `text` that is a complete `<speak>` document is passed to the engine as written.

**Say it again.** `ref` (or the `key` of a saved utterance) in place of `text` says the stored script again with another `voice`, `engine`, `format` or `hz` - a new ref, the same words and direction.

New synthesis is capped per day on each deployment (429 with `budgetExhausted` when used up); stored audio is never affected.
